<section class="pub-about" id="about" aria-label="About us">
  <p class="pub-summary">After decades as provenance and art history researchers, we have watched our field change in many ways. Computational techniques and data-driven approaches can reveal patterns, structures and dynamics that are hard to see through close reading alone. They open up research questions that were previously impossible to answer, or even to ask. We call this computational provenance: provenance research using large language models, statistics and network analysis.</p>
  <p class="pub-summary">This workshop gives researchers and practitioners a first encounter with these theories, methods and tools, so they can bring new policies, methods and techniques into their institutions and their own research. Interdisciplinary work with computer scientists and digital humanities specialists is extremely valuable, and fair, equal collaboration starts with a clear understanding of what can be done, and how.</p>
  <p class="pub-summary">Over four days, the workshop mixes teaching with a social program, all centred on provenance. Participants work on and develop their own projects and take part in conversations about the field. Alongside the sessions, we put together a social program that includes guided visits to museums and archives, where curators and provenance experts introduce their collections, and visits to provenance-related events taking place that week.</p>
  <p class="pub-summary">The workshop travels, and each edition takes place in a different part of the world: the first edition was held at Leuphana University Lüneburg, Germany, and the second at the Getty Research Institute, Los Angeles, USA. These two editions have been very successful, drawing hundreds of applications from researchers and practitioners worldwide. Each edition offers 16 places, fully funded by us.</p>
</section>
